opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that a new lab, especially one built around a genuinely different research direction, doesn't yet know what it's actually good at. You might start with a thesis, say, that a certain architecture or a certain way of thinking about interpretability or physics-inspired learning will matter, but a thesis isn't a product. You need time to find out whether the idea survives contact with real problems, at real scale, with real data.

If you rush into commercialization in month two, you end up optimizing for whatever the first customer asks for. That's very seductive, because revenue feels like validation. But early customers usually ask for incremental things, a slightly better version of what already exists. And if you say yes to that too early, the lab quietly turns into a consulting shop or a feature team, and the original research bet never gets a fair test.

Six to twelve months is roughly the window where you can run enough experiments to separate signal from noise. In the first few months you're mostly building infrastructure, hiring, getting the team to share a common language. Then you start getting results, and most of them are negative or ambiguous, which is normal. Somewhere in the second half of that period you hopefully find one or two things that are surprisingly strong, things that work better than you expected, or work in a place you didn't anticipate. That's what you want to commercialize, not your initial guess.

There's also a cultural dimension. The habits a team forms early tend to stick. If the first months are about deadlines and deliverables, it's very hard to later carve out space for open-ended exploration. If the first months are about curiosity and rigor, you can layer product discipline on top of that later. It's much harder to go in the other direction.

And honestly, from the investor side, I think the smart ones understand this. What they're buying in a new lab isn't next quarter's revenue, it's the option value of a real technical insight. Protecting that early R&D period is how you make the option worth something.

That said, I don't think it should be open-ended. Having a rough horizon, six months, twelve months, forces you to ask at the end: did we find something real? If yes, commit. If not, be honest about it and pivot. The time box is part of what makes the research period productive rather than just comfortable.

r001.rationale: It says rushing to meet early customer requests can steer the lab toward incremental work and away from giving its original research bet a fair test, describing a premature move into a worse direction.

r002.rationale: It presents the six-to-twelve-month period as time to run experiments and discover unexpectedly strong results to commercialize instead of committing to the initial guess.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first reason is that we don't actually know yet what the product is. When I was at MIT working on KAN, the whole point was that we were exploring a space where the answer wasn't obvious. If you commit to a commercial direction on day one, you're committing to your current beliefs, and your current beliefs in a new technical area are usually wrong in at least one important way. Six to twelve months is roughly the time it takes to be wrong a few times and learn something real from it.

The second reason is more about the team. A lab is a group of people who have to learn how to think together. In the early phase, the most valuable output isn't a model or a demo, it's a shared sense of taste: what counts as a good result, what problems are worth attacking, what we're willing to give up. You can't rush that. If you bolt a go-to-market plan onto a team that hasn't developed that shared taste, every decision becomes a negotiation instead of an instinct.

The third thing I'd say is that the commercialization decision is much cheaper to make well once you've done some research. If we spend six months and discover that our approach gives a real edge in, say, scientific discovery or interpretability, then the business conversation is grounded in something concrete. If we discover it doesn't, we've saved ourselves from building a company around a hypothesis that was going to fail anyway. Either way the research phase pays for itself.

I'd also push back a little on the framing that R&D and commercialization are opposites. In my experience, the best research questions come from trying to make something actually work for someone. So during those months we're still talking to people who might use what we build. We're just not letting their timelines dictate what we investigate. That's the difference: input, not control.

And frankly, there's a physics intuition here too. You want to find the ground state before you start building on top of it. If you start constructing while the system is still settling, you spend all your energy fighting the thing instead of using it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says committing to a commercial direction on day one means committing to beliefs that are likely wrong, risking an inferior direction.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes using the research period to explore an uncertain space, learn from mistaken assumptions, and discover where the work has a real edge before choosing a commercial direction.

astra-6.text:
I think a new lab needs time to figure out what it can do reliably, what it can do differently, and whether that difference matters to a customer. Those are related questions, but you can’t answer all of them with an impressive demo.

Six to twelve months gives the team room to test ideas, discover limitations, and build a shared way of doing research. If you commit to commercialization too early, a particular customer’s requirements can end up defining the entire research agenda before you’ve understood your strongest opportunity.

That doesn’t mean avoiding customers during that period. You should be talking to them and testing your assumptions. The point is to make the commercial commitment once you have evidence that the technology and the need line up. And I’d treat six to twelve months as a useful window, not a fixed rule.

r001.rationale: It says committing too early can let a customer's requirements define the research agenda before the lab understands its strongest opportunity, conveying the risk of prematurely choosing a weaker direction.

r002.rationale: It describes using the six-to-twelve-month period to test ideas, discover limitations, and identify the lab's strongest opportunity before committing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a new lab needs time to figure out what it can do uniquely well. At the beginning, you have people, ideas, and some hypotheses, but you don’t yet know which ideas will work or which capabilities will be difficult for others to reproduce.

Six to twelve months gives you room to run experiments, fail, and develop a clearer research direction. If you commit to commercialization too early, customer requests can start determining the research agenda before you’ve built a technical advantage. You may end up doing useful engineering, but miss the reason to build a research lab in the first place.

That doesn’t mean ignoring users during that period. You should be talking to them and understanding their problems. The commitment should come when you have evidence of both a technical advantage and a problem that advantage can solve. I’d treat six to twelve months as a working window, rather than a fixed rule.

r001.rationale: The response says committing too early lets customer requests set the research agenda before the lab has a technical advantage, potentially leading it to useful engineering while missing its research purpose.

r002.rationale: It describes the six-to-twelve-month period as time to experiment, learn what the lab can do uniquely well, and develop a clearer research direction.
